title: Large exchange bias from coupled antiferromagnetic order and glassy magnetic freezing in $Co_{0.36}NbS_{2}$
authors: Suman Mondal, Himadri Roy Dakua, Raz Luger, Muntaser Naamneh, Eran Maniv
abstract: Magnetization measurements on single-crystalline $Co_{0.36}NbS_{2}$ reveal antiferromagnetic order near $T_{N} \simeq 26 K$ and a lower-temperature history-dependent magnetic response consistent with glassy freezing of a subset of magnetic moments. After field cooling, $M(H)$ loops exhibit a sizable exchange-bias shift, reaching $|H_{EB}| \simeq 4.4 kOe$ at $1.8 K$ for a $70 kOe$ field-cooling sweep protocol. The training effect, field-sweep and cooling-field protocol dependence, and disappearance of the bias near a blocking temperature $T_{B} \simeq 12 K$, well below $T_{N}$, support an interpretation in which frozen uncompensated moments are exchange-coupled to an antiferromagnetic matrix. These results suggest that antiferromagnetic-glassy-moment coupling may provide a broader route to exchange bias in off-stoichiometric magnetic $NbS_{2}$ intercalates.
summary: This experimental study characterizes the large exchange bias observed in Co0.36NbS2, a material exhibiting both antiferromagnetic order and glassy magnetic freezing. The authors propose that the EB arises from the exchange coupling between the AFM background and disorder-induced, pinned uncompensated magnetic moments. This work expands the understanding of EB mechanisms beyond simple heterostructures by incorporating glassy dynamics.
main_problem: The study investigates the origin and mechanism of large exchange bias (EB) in a material where magnetic ordering is coupled with glassy magnetic freezing.
main_result: The large EB effect is attributed to the exchange coupling between long-range antiferromagnetic (AFM) order and disorder-induced, glassy frozen uncompensated magnetic moments.
method: Magnetization measurements (M(H) loops) were performed using Zero-Field-Cooled (ZFCH) and Field-Cooled (FC) protocols, along with temperature-dependent measurements.
model_or_system: The physical system is single-crystalline Co0.36NbS2, an intercalated transition-metal dichalcogenide exhibiting both AFM order (T_N ~ 26 K) and glassy freezing below a blocking temperature (T_B ~ 12 K).
key_observables: Exchange bias shift (|HEB| ~ 4.4 kOe), AFM transition temperature (T_N), blocking temperature (T_B), and the temperature dependence of irreversibility (T_irr).
important_parameters: The EB magnitude is sensitive to the field-cooling and field-sweep protocols, and the coupling is confirmed by the vanishing of EB below T_B.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the EB arises from the coupling between the established AFM matrix and a history-dependent, glassy component of magnetic moments.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate M(T) and M(H) loops showing the AFM transition and the EB shift. Phase diagrams map the coexistence of AFM and glassy regimes, and schematics detail the field-cooling mechanism.
paper_structure: The paper systematically measures magnetic properties (M(T), M(H)) across various field protocols to characterize the coexistence of AFM order and glassy freezing, culminating in a proposed model for the EB mechanism.
why_interesting: The interplay between long-range order (AFM) and quenched disorder (glassy freezing) is a canonical problem in condensed matter physics, relevant to understanding complex magnetic ground states and frustration.

(a) Temperature dependence of the magnetization measured in zero-field-cooled heating (ZFCH) and field-cooled (FC) protocols for H = 100 Oe applied along the c axis. The cusp near TN ≈26 K marks the AFM transition, while the ZFCH/FC bifurcation indicates thermomagnetic irreversibility. FIG. 3. Field-protocol and temperature dependence of the EB response. (a) EB field |HEB| and coercive field HC as a function of the field-sweep range HFS, measured at 2 K with H ∥c. In this protocol, the cooling field was set equal to the sweep field, Hcool = HFS. (b) Cooling-field dependence of |HEB| and HC at 2 K, measured using a fixed maximum field-sweep range of ±140 kOe. (c) Temperature dependence of |HEB| and HC after field cooling in 70 kOe and measuring loops with a ±70 kOe sweep range. The EB vanishes near the blocking temperature TB ≈12 K, while HC becomes small on approaching TN. Error bars represent the uncertainty estimated from the magnetic-field step size.

FIG. 4. Field dependence of magnetic irreversibility. (a)-(e) Normalized magnetization, M(T)/MFC(2 K), measured in ZFCH and FC protocols for different applied fields with H ∥c. The cusp near TN marks the AFM transition, while Tirr is defined operationally as the temperature at which the ZFCH and FC curves bifurcate. (f) Field dependence of Tirr. The solid red line is a fit to Eq. (2), giving ϕ = 5.54 ± 0.29.

FIG. 5. ZFC aging-memory response of Co0.36NbS2. The sample was cooled in zero field with a one-hour wait- ing time at selected temperatures Tw, then cooled to base temperature. Magnetization was measured on warming in H = 1 kOe and compared with a reference curve measured without a waiting step. The plotted difference, ∆M(T) = Maged(T) −Mref(T), shows memory dips near the waiting temperatures, most clearly for Tw = 10, 15, and 20 K. The dips indicate that the system retains memory of the aging temperature, consistent with slow glassy magnetic dynamics.

FIG. 6. Magnetic phase diagram and schematic exchange-bias mechanism. (a) Magnetic field- temperature phase diagram for Co0.36NbS2 with H ∥c. The upper boundary marks the AFM transition near TN, while the lower boundary follows the irreversibility tempera- ture Tirr extracted from the ZFCH/FC bifurcation. Symbols indicate experimentally determined Tirr values; shaded regions are guides to the eye. (b)-(d) Phenomenological schematic of the proposed field-cooling mechanism.
